Calculate Adaptive Landscape

Source: R/adaptive_landscape.R
adaptive_landscape.Rd

Computes the adaptive landscape (mean fitness as a function of population mean phenotype) using a fitted individual-level fitness model.

Usage

adaptive_landscape(
  data,
  fitness_model,
  trait_cols,
  group_col = NULL,
  population_variance = NULL,
  simulation_n = 1000,
  grid_n = 50,
  custom_range = NULL,
  clamp = TRUE,
  support_warn = 0.25,
  method = c("simulate", "lattice", "convolve"),
  lattice_n = 200
)

Arguments

data

A data frame containing the original trait and fitness data.

fitness_model

A fitted model object (e.g., GAM or Tps) predicting individual fitness.

trait_cols

One or two trait column names. With one trait the model is usually the $model of univariate_spline() and the result is a curve; with two it is the $model of correlated_fitness_surface() and the result is a surface.

group_col

Optional character string specifying a grouping variable.

population_variance

Optional covariance matrix for the traits. Estimated from data if NULL.

simulation_n

Integer specifying the number of individuals to simulate per grid point. Default is 1000.

grid_n

Integer specifying the resolution of the population mean grid. Default is 50.

custom_range

Optional list specifying custom ranges for the traits.

clamp

Logical; if TRUE (the default) simulated fitness from a thin-plate model (with "convolve", its fitness on the lattice) is held inside the range of the fitness type before averaging: 0 to 1 for survival, at least 0 for counts. Continuous fitness is left alone, and a GAM is unaffected because its link already respects the range. The run message says how many values were held.

support_warn

Share of the population simulated at the optimum that may fall outside the data before the optimum is flagged as extrapolated. Default is 0.25.

method

How the mean fitness of each population is worked out: "simulate" (the default), "lattice" or "convolve". See Details.

lattice_n

Nodes per trait of the lattice the "lattice" method predicts the fitness surface on, for two traits (at least 8). One trait uses max(10 * lattice_n, 1000) nodes. Default is 200.

Value

An object of class "adaptive_landscape". Its optimum_edge is TRUE when the highest mean fitness lies on the edge of the grid, where the landscape may keep rising beyond it. method is the method used (which can differ from the one asked for when it falls back), lattice describes the lattice of the "lattice" and "convolve" methods (nodes and spacing per trait, number of predictions) and lattice_check the interpolation check of the "lattice" method: draws predicted exactly, the largest error among them, the tolerance, whether it passed, the final nodes per trait, the number of refinements and the number of draws predicted directly. clipped counts the fitness values held by clamp: simulated individuals for "simulate" and "lattice", lattice nodes for "convolve".

Details

All three methods estimate the same quantity, the mean fitness of a population whose traits are normally distributed around each grid point with the within-population (co)variance:

  • "simulate" draws simulation_n individuals at every grid point, predicts the fitness of each one from the model and averages them (Monte Carlo). It is the slowest, and the answer moves a little with the random seed.

  • "lattice" makes the same random draws, in the same order, but predicts the fitness surface once on a fine lattice and interpolates it for every individual (cubic interpolation along each trait). For a seed it gives nearly the same numbers as "simulate", several times faster, and leaves the random number stream where "simulate" would. A sample of the draws is also predicted exactly to check the interpolation; the lattice is made finer if the error is more than 0.1% of the range of fitness over the grid of population means, and the result's lattice_check records it. When the lattice would need as many predictions as the draws, or a finer one would cost more than predicting the remaining draws, the draws are predicted directly as in "simulate".

  • "convolve" draws nothing. It evaluates the fitness surface on a lattice that contains every grid point and averages it with the weights of the normal distribution (a convolution), so there is no simulation noise, the landscape is smooth and the result does not depend on the seed. simulation_n is not used. The lattice is at most a quarter of each trait's SD apart, and finer when the traits are strongly correlated, and the weights reach 5 SD around each grid point (8 SD for a GAM with a log link, whose fitness can climb steeply). Its cost depends on the grid and the variance, not on simulation_n: when the distribution is very narrow next to the grid step, or the traits are almost perfectly correlated, it would need more predictions than simulating simulation_n individuals at every grid point, and the "lattice" method is used instead (with a message).

The "lattice" method interpolates a GAM on the scale of its link function and transforms the result back, so fitness stays inside the range the link allows.

For a single trait the grid also carries .ind_fit, the individual fitness function evaluated at each population mean, for drawing the two curves together (see plot_adaptive_landscape()).

The simulated populations spread beyond the data, especially towards the edge of the grid, and the fitness of those individuals is extrapolated. .outside in the grid is the share of each simulated population falling outside the convex hull of the observed trait pairs, or outside the observed range for one trait, and the result's support gives that share over the whole grid and at the optimum. With "convolve" it is the share of each population's normal distribution lying outside the data, taking the part of each lattice cell that lies outside.

Examples

prep <- prepare_selection_data(bumpus, "survival", c("total_length", "weight"))
surf <- correlated_fitness_surface(prep, "survival", c("total_length", "weight"), grid_n = 30)
#> Data type: binary; method: gam; n = 136; k = 29
#> GAM fitting with 136 observations
#>   Trying formula: main
#> Success with formula: main
#> Predictions range: 0.0472 to 0.703
#> Masked 424 of 900 grid points outside the data
land <- adaptive_landscape(prep, surf$model, c("total_length", "weight"),
                           simulation_n = 100, grid_n = 15)
#> Population mean grid ranges:
#>   total_length: -2.96 to 2.94
#>   weight: -3.12 to 4.85
#> Estimated within-population variance-covariance:
#>              total_length weight
#> total_length       1.0000 0.5839
#> weight             0.5839 1.0000
#> Calculating mean fitness for 225 grid points
#> Optimal population mean phenotype:
#>   total_length    weight
#> 8   -0.0123897 -3.121579
#> Mean fitness at optimum: 0.6796
#> The highest mean fitness is on the edge of the grid; the landscape may keep rising beyond it
#> 75% of simulated individuals fell outside the data (99% at the optimum)
#> The optimum rests on extrapolation: more than 25% of the population simulated there lies outside the data
land$optimum
#>   total_length    weight .mean_fit .outside
#> 8   -0.0123897 -3.121579 0.6795783     0.99

# one trait, from the spline fitness function
uni <- univariate_spline(prep, "survival", "total_length")
#> Fitness type detected: binary
land1 <- adaptive_landscape(prep, uni$model, "total_length", simulation_n = 100, grid_n = 30)
#> Population mean grid ranges:
#>   total_length: -2.96 to 2.94
#> Estimated within-population variance-covariance:
#>              total_length
#> total_length            1
#> Calculating mean fitness for 30 grid points
#> Optimal population mean phenotype:
#>    total_length
#> 15   -0.1140707
#> Mean fitness at optimum: 0.5731
#> 34% of simulated individuals fell outside the data (1% at the optimum)
plot_adaptive_landscape(land1, "total_length")


# the same landscape without simulation noise
land_c <- adaptive_landscape(prep, surf$model, c("total_length", "weight"),
                             grid_n = 15, method = "convolve")
#> Population mean grid ranges:
#>   total_length: -2.96 to 2.94
#>   weight: -3.12 to 4.85
#> Estimated within-population variance-covariance:
#>              total_length weight
#> total_length       1.0000 0.5839
#> weight             0.5839 1.0000
#> Calculating mean fitness for 225 grid points
#> Averaging over a lattice of 77 x 97 nodes, spacing 0.211 x 0.19
#> Optimal population mean phenotype:
#>   total_length    weight
#> 7   -0.4336396 -3.121579
#> Mean fitness at optimum: 0.6757
#> The highest mean fitness is on the edge of the grid; the landscape may keep rising beyond it
#> 76% of the populations' distribution lay outside the data (97% at the optimum)
#> The optimum rests on extrapolation: more than 25% of the population there lies outside the data
land_c$optimum
#>   total_length    weight .mean_fit  .outside
#> 7   -0.4336396 -3.121579 0.6757213 0.9688433
